entries.title: Vigil held for 7-year-old girl killed in Chatham stabbing
entries.summary: <p>A vigil was held Sunday afternoon in Chatham to honor a young girl who was stabbed to death Saturday.</p><p>Family friends and community members gathered in the 8600 block of south Cottage Grove Avenue where 7-year-old Edi Mari Hernandez Chacon was killed.</p><p>Family members, dressed in black and white, released white balloons, lit candles and scattered candy at the spot where Edi Mari was police said a woman <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/03/woman-in-custody-after-girl-7-fatally-stabbed-in-chatham" target="_blank" >attacked the child Saturday morning</a>. The girl’s loved ones shed tears and embraced each other as they circled around the candles.</p><p>Edi Mari’s family declined to speak to a Sun-Times reporter.</p><p>“It’s really sad,” said Michelle Clark, who attended the vigil to show support for the family. “I’m a mother, and I can’t imagine the pain they must be going through.”</p><p>Edi Mari was walking with her older sister just before noon when a woman approached her and stabbed her multiple times in the back, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Bystanders who witnessed the stabbing intervened and detained the woman, police said.</p><p>The girl was taken to Comer Children’s Hospital, where she was pronounced dead.</p><p>The woman, who has not been identified, suffered injuries during the scuffle with bystanders, and she was transported to the hospital before being taken into police custody.</p><p>Clark said she had seen the woman several times at a nearby train station and cannot understand what may have led her to attack a young girl.</p><p>“We need to protect children,” she said. “They deserve to be safe walking down the street.”</p><p>Chicago police had not announced charges as of Sunday evening.</p><p>“I am deeply saddened by the senseless stabbing of a 7 year old child in our neighborhood,” Ald. Michelle Harris said in a statement. “My heart goes out to her family, friends, and everyone who is affected by this horrific incident. No child should ever have to experience violence or fear while simply walking down the sidewalk.”</p>

entries.title: Bears RB Kyle Monangai bludgeons Jets in 23-12 win
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> running back Kyle Monangai was exhausted. His running mate, D’Andre Swift, was on the bench as punishment for fumbling. His right thumb hurt for some reason.</p><p>But he kept plowing forward, time after time after time. The Bears took over with 9:16 left in Sunday’s 23-12 win against the Jets at Soldier Field — and never gave the ball back.</p><p>Monangai touched the ball nine times on the drive — eight runs and one pass from fellow backup Tyson Bagent. He finished with 30 carries — the most by a Bears running back since David Montgomery had 32 in 2020 — for 146 yards.</p><p>Sunday was a boxing match in which the Bears threw nothing but jabs. Monangai served as Bears coach Ben Johnson’s left hand to bludgeon the Jets. Bagent, who took over this week as the Bears’ quarterback with Caleb Williams out, didn’t provide much of a right hook. He was solid, though, completing 25-of-34 passes — that’s 74% — for 268 yards, one interception and an 83.9 passer rating. </p><p>Not bad for a pair of second-stringers.</p><p>“We all know that we’re gonna run the football,” Monangai said. “We know it. The other team knows it. The people watching at home and in the stadium know it. … We put the time in to still stick to what we know we’re going to do. We just say, ‘You gotta come stop this.’”</p><p>The Jets could not. The Bears finished with a franchise-best 34 first downs to the Jets’ seven. They averaged a first down every 2.6 plays. They held the ball for all but 17 minutes, 15 seconds, and never punted. In the fourth quarter alone, they held the ball for all but 45 seconds.</p><p>“That’s just who we are,” tight end Cole Kmet said. “That’s our team. I think our run game and how we are at the line of scrimmage is something that can carry over throughout the entire season. Despite who we have under center, I think it shows we can beat anybody when we’re physical up front.”</p><p>Johnson marveled at Monangai’s physicality. On a day in which the Bears struggled in the red zone, he had their only two touchdowns, a one-yard, second-effort plunge on fourth down in the first quarter and a five-yarder in the third.</p><p>“That’s just one ball of muscle right there,” defensive end Dayo Odeyingbo said.</p><p>Johnson didn’t realize he gave Monangai a career-high 30 carries — it was as many as he’d had all season before Sunday — until he got back into his Soldier Field office.</p><p>“He ran really hard,” Johnson said. “He found some creases and turned on the gas. I thought I saw one really, really good stiff arm there as well.</p><p>“When you see a guy running like that, you want to feed him as the play caller. And I do think it elevates all of those guys out there and gives them a spark as well, the guy's blocking for him. And it was good to see. We needed that.”</p><p>Whether sparked by Monangai or the below-average play of the opposition, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/04/chicago-bears-defense-jets-ben-johnson-tyson-bagent-kyle-monangai-dillon-thieneman-geno-smith-isaiah-williams" target="_blank" >Bears’ defense dominated</a>, giving up seven first downs on eight possessions. Four of the Jets’ eight drives went for six yards or less. Swift ran inspired, too, totaling 58 yards on 15 carries. His third-quarter fumble at the Bears’ 28 kept the Jets in the game — they’d kick a field goal to pull within seven — and got the running back benched the rest of the way. Roschon Johnson had four carries from then on to fill in for Monangai.</p><p>The Bears are the NFL’s best rushing team, and Swift and Monangai the best running back duo. They’re the seventh NFL duo since 1950 — and the first since 1976 — to each have at least 300 rushing yards through the season’s first four games.</p><p>“Keep the defense off the field,” right tackle Darnell Wright said. “Control the football. … Put it in our hands. Good results.”</p><p>After 38-year-old third-stringer Case Keenum captured the sport’s imagination Monday night, Johnson refused to publicly name a starting quarterback. When Keenum found out it would be Bagent, he wanted to be the one to tell him — and did at Halas Hall on Wednesday morning after asking him to come into work early.</p><p>“Tyson's earned the right to be our No. 2 quarterback,” Johnson said. “I have a lot of confidence in him, thought he played really well today. Efficient with the football.”</p><p>The one exception: when he threw a second-quarter interception to Minkah Fitzpatrick, who ended the Jets’ NFL-record 21-game streak without an interception.</p><p>Bagent wasn’t technically the starter — Johnson put Keenum at quarterback and split Bagent wide on the first play of the game. Keenum pitched the ball to Swift and left the game for good, with the coach later describing it as akin to the ceremonial first pitch. That was the only detail that kept the Bears from becoming the first team since the 1997 Jaguars to have three starting quarterbacks win a game in the first four weeks of the season. </p><p>Barring a quick return from Williams, Bagent lines up to make next week’s start in Green Bay. Whether he’ll have Monangai by his side depends on the running back’s right thumb; he had imaging done after the game, and the Bears figure to give him a diagnosis Monday. Monangai didn't seem too concerned.</p><p>Either way, the Bears' run game will travel.</p><p>“For everybody, it's pretty easy to get excited and juiced up for that one,” Bagent said. “Which, I'm sure, they will be, too.”</p>

entries.title: Vikings stay unbeaten, top winless Dolphins 15-10
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS — The Minnesota Vikings stayed undefeated with more dominance by their defense and five field goals from Will Reichard, sidestepping their early passing game problems to secure a 15-10 victory over the winless Miami Dolphins on Sunday.</p><p>T.J. Hockenson had a career-high-tying 13 receptions for 119 yards on 13 targets from Kyler Murray, including the game-sealing 8-yard catch on third-and-5 from the 10. Hockenson was wide open and could've coasted into the end zone, but he wisely slid in front of the goal line to drain the clock down to the two-minute warning.</p><p>With the Dolphins out of timeouts, the Vikings had Murray take three straight kneel-downs to move to 4-0 for the second time in three years.</p><p>The Dolphins, who are 0-4 for the first time since 2019 in their first season under coach Brian Flores, were crushed by a combination of unforced mistakes and a bit of bad luck.</p><p>New Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis went just 9 for 17 for 85 yards, losing a fumble during one of the two sacks by Dallas Turner. Willis thought he had escaped the relentless Vikings pass rush to float a 68-yard touchdown pass to Chris Bell early in the second quarter, but Bell was flagged for illegal touching after stepping out of bounds as he moved to get open while Willis scrambled toward the sideline.</p><p>The Vikings had 11 penalties for 85 yards, but they dodged a costly flag when Ivan Pace Jr. had a call for roughing the kicker waved off when the video replay assist system determined he tipped Bradley Pinion's punt and therefore didn't commit a penalty.</p><p>After netting just 76 yards on 21 plays in the first half and failing to finish any possession across midfield, the Dolphins finally found a couple of creases in Minnesota's otherwise-suffocating defense directed by Flores, who's in his fourth year as coordinator.</p><p>Ollie Gordon, in an elevated role following the season-ending knee injury to star running back De'Vone Achane, ripped off a career-long 53-yard run on third-and-5 to set up Riley Patterson's 27-yard field goal. Gordon had a 12-yard touchdown run on the next drive to pull the Dolphins within 12-10 late in the third quarter.</p><p>Reichard, who stretched the NFL's longest active streak to 31 consecutive made field goals, drew a loud roar from the otherwise restless crowd at U.S. Bank Stadium when he was shown on the videoboard during the two-minute warning.</p><p>Murray finished 27 for 37 for 247 yards without a turnover, but he took four sacks for 34 yards against a Dolphins defense that had none in the first three games and was often tentative and unsteady in the pocket until Hockenson helped him open up the field with a handful of clutch and difficult catches.</p><p>Aaron Jones also carried another heavy load with 20 carries for 94 yards and four receptions for 34 yards, with the Vikings missing star wide receiver Justin Jefferson (ankle) for the first time since Week 12 of the 2023 season and running back Jordan Mason (thumb) for the third game in a row.</p><h3>Injury report</h3><h3></h3><p><b>Miami:</b> Starting safety Dante Trader (knee) was hurt in the second quarter and returned after halftime.</p><p><b>Minnesota:</b> LG Donovan Jackson (knee) was sidelined in the first quarter. LT Christian Darrisaw (neck) was hurt in the second quarter after going head-first into the pile at the end of a run, returning after halftime only to be pulled again in the fourth quarter for concussion evaluation.</p><h3>Up next</h3><h3></h3><p>Miami hosts Cincinnati next Sunday.</p><p>Minnesota plays at New Orleans next Sunday.<br></p>

entries.title: What you need to know about Chicago’s historic school board election
entries.summary: <p>This fall, Chicagoans will vote for members of the city’s first fully elected school board. Every eligible Chicagoan can cast two votes (yes, two!) — one for a candidate in your school board district, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/" target="_blank" >based on your home address</a>, and a second time for school board president.</p><h3><b>How can I vote in school board elections?</b></h3><p>All voters, whether they have students in Chicago Public Schools or not, can cast ballots in the school board elections.</p><p>They are on the ballot in the Nov. 3 general election. <a class="Link" href="https://ova.elections.il.gov/" target="_blank" ><u>Online voter registration</u></a> is available until Oct. 18 and same-day registration is allowed at the polls. <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoelections.gov/voting/your-voter-information" target="_blank" ><u>Check your voter registration status here</u></a>. You must be 18 on election day, a U.S. citizen, and have lived at your current address for 30 days.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicagoelections.gov/voting/early-votingvote-centers" target="_blank" ><u>Early voting</u></a> began Oct. 1 at the Downtown Voting Supersite at 137 S. State St. and the Chicago Board of Elections Offices at 69 W. Washington St., Sixth Floor. Additional <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoelections.gov/voting/early-votingvote-centers" target="_blank" ><u>early voting sites in all 50 wards</u></a> open Oct. 19. </p><p>On Election Day Nov. 3, polls are open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m. Find your <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoelections.gov/voting/your-voter-information" target="_blank" >assigned precinct polling place here</a>.</p><h3><b>How many school board seats are up for election?</b></h3><p>All 21 seats on the Chicago Board of Education are on the ballot. Each voter can pick their local representative on the board and the person they want to be school board president.</p><p>There are 41 candidates, plus four write-ins. Four people are running for school board president.</p><p>The city is divided into 20 electoral districts — 1a, 1b, etc.. You can look up which one you live in here. The president is elected citywide and will serve a four-year term until 2030.</p><p>When the new school board is seated in January, it will replace a board that is partially elected and partially appointed. That hybrid board, launched after elections in November 2024, was the first step toward the fully elected school board.</p><p>Half of the board members will serve four-year terms and the other half will serve two years. <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/documents/legislation/ilcs/documents/010500050K34-3.htm" target="_blank" ><u>Per state law</u></a>, members elected to replace mayoral appointees will serve two years, while those in districts that had elections in 2024 will serve four years. The term lengths will swap starting in 2028.</p><h3><b>What does the school board do? </b></h3><p>School board members are responsible for the education of about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/09/24/chicago-public-schools-enrollment-drops-by-more-than-11-000-accelerating-long-term-downward-trend" >305,000 children</a> at more than 600 schools and set priorities for Chicago Public Schools.</p><p>Chicagoans are probably most familiar with one of the board’s core functions: making financial decisions. The school board can raise local property taxes and decide how to spend state and federal funding.</p><p>In the last year, the board stepped into new territory when it amended the budget prepared by CPS leaders, bucking their warnings. A narrow majority of members <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/08/12/cps-says-it-cannot-reverse-all-layoffs/" target="_blank" ><u>voted to rescind hundreds of staff layoffs</u></a> and instead build in a revenue assumption that Illinois lawmakers would provide <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/30/chicago-school-board-approves-budget-that-reverses-layoffs-but-counts-on-shaky-state-funds" >$150 million more</a> than they had already allocated.</p><p>Another key board power is <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/03/30/chicago-board-of-education-hires-macquline-king/" target="_blank" ><u>hiring a CEO/superintendent</u></a> and later evaluating their performance.</p><p>The board also votes to close and open schools, the academic calendar, and on which buildings get upgrades. It also approves contracts, including collective bargaining agreements, and contracts with charter school operators.</p><p>In Chicago, the board now has power to gather <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/08/13/chicago-public-schools-board-backs-revenue-referendums/" target="_blank" ><u>community input through referendums</u></a>.</p><p>Board members are not paid.</p><h3><b>Why didn’t Chicago always vote for school board members?</b></h3><p>Since 1995, the mayor has appointed Chicago’s school board members. Before that, there was typically a nomination process to place members on the board.</p><p>Outside Chicago, most <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/02/17/nx-s1-5717076/americas-school-boards-in-2026" target="_blank" ><u>school boards in Illinois and across the U.S.</u></a> are elected.</p><p>But over the last two decades in Chicago, demand for an elected board grew with prominent organizations such as <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2021/7/30/22602068/illinois-governor-approves-elected-chicago-school-board/" target="_blank" ><u>the Chicago Teachers Union championing the change</u></a> to hold the board accountable to families and educators. Several decisions by the appointed board had soured public perceptions of the governing body, including its unanimous vote approving <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2025/06/13/chicago-public-schools-declining-enrollment-causes-small-schools-high-costs/" target="_blank" ><u>former Mayor Rahm Emanuel’s plan to close about 50 schools</u></a>.</p><p>The bill creating the elected school board <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2021/6/16/22537184/chicago-elected-school-board-bill-clears-hurdle-but-questions-remain/" target="_blank" ><u>passed in 2021</u></a>.</p><p>The implementation was rocky in Springfield, and it faced <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2021/3/25/22351382/chicago-elected-school-board-bill-gains-momentum-calls-grow-for-another-option/" target="_blank" ><u>pushback from some local groups and former Chicago Mayor Lori Lightfoot</u></a> as it slowly got off the ground. As part of the path to a fully elected board, lawmakers required <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2024/09/25/cps-school-board-november-election-voter-guide-meet-the-candidates/" target="_blank" ><u>half the board to be elected</u></a> in 2024. The other half remained mayoral appointees, with the mayor retaining a majority.</p><p><i>Becky Vevea is the bureau chief for Chalkbeat Chicago. Makiya Seminera is a Chalkbeat reporter covering how the state and federal government affect education in Chicago and across Illinois. Emmanuel Camarillo is an education reporter for the Chicago Sun-Times.</i></p>

entries.title: Palestine Fest comes to Bridgeview for its fourth year. 'I just love being around our people"
entries.summary: <p>The fourth annual Palestine Fest in southwest suburban Bridgeview brought together a peaceful crowd looking to celebrate and enjoy Palestinian culture.</p><p>The festival, held in the parking lot of SeatGeek Stadium, also drew the attention of far-right activist Jake Lang and a small group of other far-right protesters, who clashed with a much larger crowd of counter-protesters outside a gas station near the stadium.</p><p>Protesters screamed at each other through blow horns and threw water bottles. Broadview police officers and Illinois State Police troopers managed to mostly keep the two groups separated. At least two protesters were detained. After about two hours, protesters from both sides started trickling out of the the area. </p><p>But inside the festival grounds, all was calm Sunday afternoon. Palestinian music played over loudspeakers. Families milled about. Kids rode amusement park rides. Vendors sold a range of Palestinian food and clothing.</p><p>Ablah Maali was selling handmade beaded bracelets at one of the booths Sunday. entries.title: Dear Abby: Partner's married daughters are allowed to visit whenever they want
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I've been in a relationship with a man for three years and living with him for the past two. He has two married daughters and seven grandkids. Before I entered his life, he had an open-door policy. He allowed them to visit whenever they wanted, and they still have keys to his house.</p><p>My partner and I are not on the same page regarding boundaries and privacy. While I understand the importance of children spending time with their parents, his daughters visit him two to three times a week.</p><p>I work full time, and yesterday, after a long day at the office, I arrived home at 6 p.m. to find his youngest daughter and her three kids there with the house in disarray. They stayed for dinner and lingered afterward.</p><p>I was exhausted, so I went to bed around 8 p.m., but as I lay there, I couldn't help thinking it might be time for me to move out or leave the relationship entirely. I've often felt like I don't have a voice when it comes to living in his house and that my feelings don't seem to matter. Am I wrong to feel this way? — <i>INVADED IN IOWA</i></p><p><b>DEAR INVADED:</b> No, you are not. What your gentleman friend and his children haven't taken into account is that he no longer lives alone, and an additional person needs to be considered. If, after working a full day, you don't feel up to entertaining his children and grandchildren, you should at least have some warning about what you will be facing when you get home. That you weren't consulted was inconsiderate.</p><p>If, after you have discussed this, he continues to do it without consulting you, you should absolutely get a place of your own. Continue to see him if that's an option, but create some distance.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I've had a core group of friends for almost 20 years. Some have kids, but I do not. We all met doing theater. I considered many of them my closest friends. Last month, six of them, all of whom have kids the same age, founded a new theater company, which is cool, but I was not notified or consulted.</p><p>I've acted in and stage-managed many shows with all of them, as well as played music for their shows. They're now producing a musical with my other best friend from out of state. Why am I being excluded? Am I crazy for feeling upset that I'm not being included? Is it because I don't have kids and they do? Should I just move on and find new friends? — <i>THEATER GUY</i></p><p><b>DEAR THEATER GUY:</b> You are not crazy for feeling left out. As to why they didn't mention this venture to you, I'm not the person you should ask. Is this a youth-oriented theater company? If so, they may have assumed you would not want to participate. Now that you know about it, offer to help with the show. If they decline, that would be your moment to inquire about the reasons.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Video gambling saturates Chicago area — nearly 80% of region allows video slots
entries.summary: <p>Not even 20 years ago, video gambling was illegal in the Chicago region and the rest of Illinois.</p><p>Today, nearly 80% of the six-county metropolitan area has legalized video gambling, a level of saturation that means more than 200 municipalities now allow it to varying degrees, while more than 60 communities ban the machines, according to a Chicago Sun-Times examination that also found:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-863b5ba2-bc3d-11f1-a70e-f35c7d6bc731"><li>Wealthy suburbs generally outlaw video gambling — with the North Shore communities of Evanston, Glencoe, Highland Park, Highwood, Kenilworth, Lake Bluff, Lake Forest, Wilmette and Winnetka all with prohibitions — while lower-income south suburbs generally allow it, including Dixmoor and Ford Heights.<br></li><li>Some communities are rethinking their policies. North Chicago is tightening restrictions to “reduce the amount of gaming in town,” an official says. Bolingbrook recently scrapped a ban, legalizing video slots following a referendum. In Winfield, an advisory referendum is planned in the spring to gauge public support for keeping or lifting a ban.<br></li><li>Virtually every town in Kane, McHenry and Will counties now allows video gambling, while most of the municipal bans are concentrated in Cook, DuPage and Lake counties. The highest concentration of prohibitions are in DuPage and Lake, where nearly 40% of communities outlaw video gambling.<br></li><li>Many municipalities with casinos also allow video gambling elsewhere in town, including Elgin, Joliet and Waukegan but not Des Plaines. Next door in Rosemont, which wasn’t allowed to host a casino two decades ago because of concerns by regulators of reputed mob influence, there is a small amount of video gambling.<br></li><li>Some communities allow so-called “gaming cafes,” which are akin to mini-casinos, while others prohibit or restrict establishments where gambling is the main draw and revenue source over, for example, food and drinks. For some suburbs, it’s a moot point, as there are no establishments in town where video gambling could exist.</li></ul><p>There’s “no video gambling in Wayne,” said Patti Engstrom, the village clerk in the far west suburb. “We have no public gathering areas, no gas stations, no mini marts, no bars, no restaurants, no commercial whatsoever. We are an equestrian community. We have horses, not commercial businesses.”</p><p>For many years, video gambling devices were allowed in Chicago-area establishments only if they were used for “amusement” purposes and didn’t pay winnings — though many illicitly did in concert with the mob that controlled much of that underground industry.</p><p>An Illinois law legalizing video gambling terminals, or VGTs, was enacted in 2009, and the machines went live for “patron play” in September 2012.</p><p>“At the end of 2012, Illinois had 2,290 terminals generating $12.3 million in revenue,” according to a report from the Illinois Municipal League, which represents local governments.</p><p>“By 2025, the state had more than 49,000 terminals producing $3.19 billion in net terminal income revenue, resulting in nearly $1.12 billion in tax revenue, including $160 million distributed to municipalities and counties, and significant profits for video gaming establishments and terminal operators.”</p><p>The Illinois Gaming Board reports as of early September, “there are 8,799 video gaming locations and 50,049 VGTs and Illinois remains the largest regulated, distributed video gaming network of its kind in the world.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-740000" name="html-embed-module-740000"></a><div style="min-height:790px" id="datawrapper-vis-QHkjY"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/QHkjY/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-QHkjY"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/QHkjY/full.png" alt="A map of the collar counties of northeast Illinois, with several small dots placed throughout, all of the same size. Most of those that do not are clustered in the northern suburbs of Chicago, on either side of the border of Cook County and Lake County, especially toward the lake." /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Ramifications of video gambling saturation</h3><p>Regulating gambling statewide, the government agency reports to Gov. JB Pritzker, who declined to say whether he believes video gambling has become too ubiquitous in Illinois — and brings about too many negative impacts.</p><p>Beyond gambling addiction, the vastness of video gambling also has the potential to normalize gambling for children, who are exposed to marketing. Studies show many who gamble are those who can least afford it. And video gambling is fueling a crime wave of after-hour burglaries at establishments with the machines.</p><p>“I was born here in 1980, I was living here when they were authorized, I’ve got 40 years of sort of a time lapse to watch,” said Ben Huizenga of the nonprofit Stop Predatory Gambling Illinois. “It has absolutely changed the face of our region, it’s changed what people do with their time.</p><p>“It’s really this kind of invisible parasite on the economy in Illinois.”</p><p>A trade group representing the video gambling industry didn't return calls.</p><p> Pritzker became governor in early 2019, so he didn’t sign the legislation legalizing video gambling.</p><p>But the billionaire Democrat who's toying with a presidential run did sign other legislation that vastly expanded other types of gambling in Illinois, from sports wagering to new casinos.</p><p>Running for a third term in the Nov. 3 general election, Pritzker’s personal investments have included gambling assets over the years, with a past interest in casinos in Elgin, Indiana, the Niagara Falls area and possibly beyond.</p><p>A spokesman for Pritzker’s Republican opponent, Darren Bailey, said local governments “have the ability to opt in” or out of video gambling and “regulate the number of VGTs” and, if elected, he “would keep it that way.”</p><p>Asked whether video gambling has expanded too far, a gaming board spokeswoman said: “Opining or speculating about economic trends in gaming markets and issues involving video gaming saturation are beyond the scope of the IGB’s regulatory and law enforcement mission. The IGB does not conduct market forecasting, provide analysis of economic trends in the Illinois gaming industry, or opine about potential market saturation.”</p><p>Huizenga said, “I’d say we’re actually at the point that we have about as many VGTs as Illinois can absorb.</p><h3>Role sweepstakes machines play</h3><p>While VGTs are regulated, there are similar devices, called sweepstakes machines, that are largely unregulated and located throughout the region, much to the chagrin of the gaming board.</p><p>The agency's "view is that 'sweepstakes' machines are illegal gambling devices that lack supervision by any regulatory body, have no oversight or licensing of any of the establishments, operators or associated individuals," the spokeswoman said. entries.title: Lincolnwood man 'exploited the trust of the Orthodox Jewish religious community' in alleged fraud scheme
entries.summary: <p>Federal authorities are accusing a 27-year-old Lincolnwood resident of overseeing an investment fraud scheme that “exploited the trust of the Orthodox Jewish religious community” — whose members may have lost several million dollars in the alleged scam.</p><p>The complaint was recently filed by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission against Jacob Garfinkel and his Skokie business enterprise known as 5G Funding that was said to “make short-term, high-interest loans to small businesses secured by a portion of the businesses’ future receivables,” court records show.</p><p>“Garfinkel claimed that 5G Funding’s business was highly profitable, and that he and the investors would split the net profits that 5G Funding generated from merchant cash advances that the investors funded,” according to the complaint, filed in U.S. District Court in Chicago.</p><p>The complaint alleges that while Garfinkel “did use some investor funds to engage in an unprofitable merchant cash advance business, he misled investors about the nature and amount of his compensation and collected $1.1 million in ‘origination fees’ out of 5G Funding’s merchant cash advances.”</p><p>“He also diverted another approximately $1 million in merchant repayments and other funds that he represented would be used to benefit 5G Funding investors, and not himself. Garfinkel diverted these funds for his personal spending and for transfers to related parties.”</p><p>Garfinkel and his business “made multiple other misrepresentations to investors,” according to the SEC, which regulates the financial sector. Among the claims: that “he had a track record of generating returns in the merchant cash advance industry.”</p><p>Garfinkel “solicited investments in 5G Funding from friends, neighbors, and word-of-mouth referrals from existing investors, almost exclusively within Orthodox Jewish communities in Illinois, New York and New Jersey.”</p><p>“Investors trusted Garfinkel due to their social or community connections with him. Some investors based their decision to invest on their oral and written communications with Garfinkel about the investment, recommendations from existing 5G Funding investors, and their trust in Garfinkel.”</p><h3>The newly filed SEC case</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/8f/27/04dea14c4fcb81b5b008ae2ce2b0/garfinkel.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Garfinkel is accused of diverting around $320,000 in “additional merchant cash advance repayments that should have been paid to 5G Funding investors to an account he controlled in the name of JCG Consulting.”</p><p>“Garfinkel was the sole signatory on JCG Consulting’s bank account and used it for his personal expenses, including using it to pay a down payment on a home, to pay his personal gambling expenses, and to purchase cars and watches,” according to the SEC.</p><p>Garfinkel’s attorney, Ariel Weissberg, said: “Mr. Garfinkel will not have any comment as to the current proceedings other than that he denies any wrongful conduct.”</p><p>All told, Garfinkel and his business are accused of raising around $4.5 million from investors, with less than $1.7 million returned — meaning about $2.8 million was allegedly lost.</p><p>Of the 23 investors in the scheme, 22 allegedly lost money, with those losses between $15,000 and $670,000.</p><p>The SEC’s complaint accused Garfinkel and his business of violating anti-fraud provisions of federal law and is seeking a judgment that would bar Garfinkel “from again offering or selling securities” and claw back “ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest” and impose “civil monetary penalties.”</p><p>While the SEC proceeding is a civil matter, sources say there is also a criminal investigation into Garfinkel, though federal authorities wouldn’t comment.</p><p>The U.S. attorney’s office and SEC have been involved in other proceedings against another man who’s accused of scamming members of the Orthodox Jewish community in the Chicago region: Rabbi Zvi Feiner.</p><h3>Rabbi Feiner’s recent plea agreement</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dc/99/67933b324d80a4fd1579bdc349de/feiner2.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Filed in 2019, the SEC case accused Feiner and another man of operating “a fraudulent scheme involving the misappropriation of proceeds raised through the offer and sale of membership interests in limited liability companies ... that would purchase, own, and sell nursing homes and assisted living facilities.”</p><p>“Feiner is an ordained Orthodox Jewish rabbi and was a well-regarded figure in the Orthodox Jewish community on Chicago’s north side and near north suburbs. As such, he exploited those relationships by soliciting members of the Orthodox Jewish community to invest in his scheme.”</p><p>Among them: an elderly Holocaust survivor, who invested more than $1 million, court records show.</p><p>That SEC case is essentially on hold while a parallel criminal case is underway, though that appears to be winding down. Feiner recently pleaded guilty to wire fraud, while other charges are expected to be dismissed.</p><p>He has yet to be sentenced, but prosecutors are recommending no prison time or fine.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2019/9/23/20880921/rabbi-accused-fraud-nursing-home-deals" target="_blank" >Rabbi accused of fraud in nursing home deals</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/04/23/metropolitan-bank-trust-chicago-fdic-takeover-collapse-zvi-feiner-sol-barket-obriens-restaurant" target="_blank" >Before regulators closed North Loop bank, millions in loans to Chicago rabbi, developer went uncollected</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/05/04/orthodox-jewish-community-child-sexual-abuse-north-side-rabbi" target="_blank" >Little-known court case hints at larger issues in Orthodox Jewish community — child sexual abuse and secrecy</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

From there, he will come to Chicago on Oct. 18 for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/09/17/chicago-international-film-festival-2026-lineup-carrie-coon-marlon-wayans" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago International Film Festival</u></a>, appearing at a screening of his new documentary, “Bob and David Climb Machu Picchu,” co-starring friend and fellow comedian David Cross, at Music Box Theatre.</p><p>In an interview, Odenkirk, 63, reflected on his 40-year career, which has taken him from the “Saturday Night Live” writers’ room to a celebrated role as Saul Goodman on “Breaking Bad” to action movies. He said his professional decisions are more intentional than ever, following a 2021 heart attack.</p><p>But the Los Angeles-based actor retains a thirst for experimenting and challenging himself.</p><p>“I’m sort of trying to figure out, who am I, really?” said Odenkirk, who has two kids with his wife, <a class="Link" href="https://people.com/who-is-naomi-odenkirk-bob-odenkirk-wife-8416348" target="_blank" ><u>Naomi</u></a>, who works as a producer and talent manager.</p><p>“I've actually gotten to do the things I love to do and the things I just found interesting, but didn't love that much. And I’ve got to figure out what I want to do with the rest of my time. You’ve got to make big choices so you’re spending your time wisely.”</p><h3><b>‘I don’t like living without comedy’ </b></h3><p>Odenkirk addresses this “crossroads” in his career in “Bob and David Climb Machu Picchu,” directed by Michael LaHaie. It's going to be very hard, and I hope I do it right. in the new documentary “Bob and David Climb Machu Picchu,” screening at the Chicago International Film Festival.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Stuart Fero</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>When it comes to acting, Odenkirk likes a challenge, which is why he enjoyed portraying Saul Goodman, an eccentric, morally compromised lawyer, for several years.</p><p>“I didn't train as an actor,” he said. “It took all my focus and thought and effort and craft. And I learned an incredible amount about acting. It took everything I had to pull that off.”</p><p>Though “Better Call Saul” contained scenes of tension and violence, Odenkirk said he was grateful for the humor that the showrunners and writers infused in the show.</p><p>“I don’t like living without comedy,” he said. “Whenever Saul is making a TV commercial, he's having the time of his life. I loved when that character got to have fun. Those things saved me.”</p><h3><b>Finding the right fit on and Off-Broadway </b></h3><p>Odenkirk said he also evaluates the tone of a script when seeking out theatrical roles.</p><p>“I was considering a really well-written Broadway show, and I just was like, ‘It's too dramatic, it's too sad, it's just too much of a downer,’” he said. “I couldn't do it.”</p><p>There are elements of dark humor in Odenkirk’s roles in “Glengarry Glen Ross” and Eric Bentley's “Are You Now or Have You Ever Been,” which runs through Sept. 11 at New York City Center Stage I. The latter depicts real-life figures, from Arthur Miller to Paul Robeson, who were subpoenaed to testify before the 1940s House Committee on Un-American Activities. The rotating cast performed dialogue pulled entirely from actual transcripts of the hearings.</p><p>In a limited run last summer, Odenkirk portrayed actor Lionel Stander, who was accused of being a communist and blacklisted from Hollywood. entries.title: Bronzeville cultural zone to feature museums, arts
entries.summary: <p>A network of eight community leaders says it has raised $75 million to help build or redevelop nine Bronzeville cultural sites and solidify the neighborhood as a national destination for the arts. The sites include the National Museum of Gospel Music, Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley House, and a recreational Bronzeville Trail.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.bronzevillelegacycollective.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Bronzeville Legacy Collective</u></a>, which is the group behind the effort, is trying to raise more amid cuts to federal arts funding for projects that appear to champion diversity, equity and inclusion. Ultimately, the collective has a long-term goal to raise $250 million, which includes $100 million for the Bronzeville Trail to be constructed from 40th and Federal Streets to 41st Street and Lake Park Avenue by 2034.</p><p>Other sites on the cultural map include a food hub called Bronzeville Cookin’, the Muddy Waters MOJO Museum, the forthcoming Deeply Rooted Center for Black Dance and Creative Communities, a new home for Definition Theatre, The Forum arts and culture complex, and the South Side Community Art Center.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-1c0000" name="html-embed-module-1c0000"></a><div style="min-height:631px" id="datawrapper-vis-EsElF"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/EsElF/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-EsElF"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/EsElF/full.png" alt="Bronzeville community leaders lay out plans to boost neighborhood’s cultural sites (Locator map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>To help spread the word, the group on Thursday arranged a bus tour of the destinations for some of Chicago’s top donors, who gathered in the garden outside of Waters’ home, viewed blueprints inside Bronzeville Cookin’ and had lunch while listening to live ragtime in the nearly 130-year-old Forum Hall performance space.</p><p>Among the invitees were co-hosts the Pritzker Pucker Family Foundation, Field Foundation and the Local Initiatives Support Corporation. Attendees also included Ald. Pat Dowell (3rd) and representatives from the MacArthur Foundation,<b> </b>the Richard H. Driehaus Foundation and Chicago’s Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events.</p><p>Members of the collective contend the investment will bring tourism to Bronzeville and other parts of entries.title: '¿¡Dónde está la ambulancia!?': tenso intercambio de policías y despachadores luego de que niña es apuñalada mortalmente
entries.summary: <p>Un hombre corrió detrás de una mujer de Calumet Heights y la dejó inconsciente después de que, al parecer, esta apuñaló mortalmente a una niña de 7 años en un ataque aparentemente sin provocación el sábado en el vecindario de Chatham.</p><p>Una multitud grande y enfurecida se formó alrededor de Edi Mari Hernández Chacón mientras se encontraba desangrándose en una acera, después de que Shavon Gayden, de 48 años, presuntamente apuñaló a la niña mientras caminaba con su hermana en la cuadra 8600 al sur de Cottage Grove Avenue, poco antes del mediodía, según la policía y el radio de los despachadores.</p><p>“La agresora se acercó desde el sur y, sin provocación, sacó un cuchillo y comenzó a apuñalar a la víctima”, señala un informe de la Policía de Chicago obtenido por el Sun-Times.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d90000" name="module-d90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“La agresora luego continuó hacia el norte, donde ciudadanos desconocidos intentaron retenerlo antes de que llegara la policía”, dice el informe.</p><p>Cuando Gayden se alejó, un hombre entre la multitud corrió tras ella y la dejó inconsciente al golpearla, dijeron los despachadores mientras se desarrollaba la caótica y desgarradora escena.</p><p>Después del ataque, un grupo de testigos conmocionados y enfurecidos se aglomeró, rodeando a la niña mientras los agentes lograban llegar hasta ella, según los despachadores, que pidieron repetidamente más oficiales en el lugar.</p><p>“¿¡Dónde está la ambulancia!?”, le exigió con tensión un agente a un despachador, mientras otros oficiales detenían la hemorragia de la niña levantándole la cabeza. “Sigue respirando”, le dijo otro agente al despachador.</p><p>Los agentes gritaron la mejor ruta para que la ambulancia llegara, y una llegó en unos 10 minutos. La policía resguardó el área y bloqueó el tráfico para que la ambulancia pudiera llegar al hospital.</p><p>La policía escoltó la ambulancia —un carro patrulla delante y otro detrás— hasta el Hospital Infantil Comer.</p><p>Edi Mari fue declarada muerta a la 1:01 p.m. el sábado, según la policía.</p><p>Una <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/en-memoria-de-eddimar-hernandez-chacon" target="_blank" >recaudación de fondos</a> lanzada para Edi Mari había superado los $1,700 la mañana del lunes.</p><p>La policía anunció cargos contra Gayden, un cargo de asesinato en primer grado, horas después de que los seres queridos de Edi Mari hicieran una vigilia el domingo por la tarde para honrar la vida de la niña.</p><p>Familiares, amigos y miembros de la comunidad se reunieron en el lugar donde Edi Mari fue asesinada. Los familiares de la niña, vestidos de blanco y negro, soltaron globos blancos, encendieron velas y esparcieron dulces en el lugar donde Gayden atacó a la niña el sábado por la mañana. Los seres queridos de la niña derramaron lágrimas y se abrazaron mientras se reunían alrededor de las veladoras.</p><p>La familia de Edi Mari se negó a hablar con una reportera del Sun-Times.</p><p>“Es realmente triste”, dijo Michelle Clark, quien asistió a la vigilia para mostrar apoyo a la familia. “Soy madre, y no puedo imaginar el dolor por el que deben estar pasando”.</p><p>Los transeúntes que presenciaron el apuñalamiento intervinieron y detuvieron a la mujer, dijo la policía.</p><p>Gayden sufrió heridas durante el forcejeo con los transeúntes, y fue trasladada al hospital antes de quedar bajo custodia policial.</p><p>Clark dijo que había visto a Gayden varias veces en una estación de tren cercana y no logra entender qué pudo haberla llevado a atacar a una niña pequeña.</p><p>“Necesitamos proteger a los niños”, dijo. “Merecen estar seguros al caminar por la calle”.</p><p>Se espera que Gayden comparezca ante la corte el lunes para una audiencia de detención.</p><p>“Estoy profundamente entristecida por el apuñalamiento sin sentido de una niña de 7 años en nuestro vecindario”, dijo la concejal Michelle Harris en un comunicado. “Mi corazón está con su familia, sus amigos y todos los afectados por este horrible incidente. Ningún niño debería tener que experimentar violencia o miedo simplemente por caminar por la acera”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: White Sox set lineup for ALDS Game 2 matchup against Guardians and right-hander Gavin Williams
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND – Just three weeks ago in this same ballpark, the White Sox had a potentially season-defining matchup against the Guardians and their towering right-hander Gavin Williams, and it even featured Sean Burke pitching behind an opener.</p><p>Tristan Peters ended Williams’ night with an 18-pitch battle that ended in a walk, and keyed a six-run White Sox’ sixth, while Burke allowed one unearned run in five innings of an eventual 7-3 win.</p><p>The Sox lineup for Game 2 of the American League Division Series on Monday offers only small variations from their previous gameplan.</p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-0a242980-c0e2-11f1-9e37-cdc3b73ee728" start="1"><li>Sam Antonacci, LF</li><li>Kyle Teel, C</li><li>Miguel Vargas, 3B</li><li>Munetaka Murakami, 1B</li><li>Andrew Benintendi, DH</li><li>Tristan Peters, CF</li><li>Braden Montgomery, RF</li><li>Chase Meidroth, 2B</li><li>Colson Montgomery, SS</li></ol><p>Literally the only difference is that Colson and Braden Montgomery (no relation) have switched places in the batting order. The switch-hitting Braden Montgomery is a candidate to be pinch-hit for against left-handed relievers, the lefty-swinging Colson Montgomery who actually performed better against southpaws all year and only has the light-hitting Luisangel Acuna who can man shortstop in his stead, is less of one.</p><p>Even Sox manager Will Venable is talking about the matchup similar to how he did in September.</p><p>“I don't know how anyone hits Gavin Williams,” Venable said. “You're going to have to cover a number of different pitches. You're going to have to foul some pitches off. You're going to have to find a way to put some balls in play and make it tough on him to get through our lineup.”</p><p>The White Sox will have left-hander Anthony Kay open the game for them on the mound, with Burke slated to follow at some point, but not necessarily immediately after Kay is done.</p><p>“We're just going to kind of feel out the game, and whenever my name gets called to pitch, I'll be ready to go,” Burke said. “The way we're doing this is really just like a team effort from the pitching side.”</p><p>Notably, the Guardians have not taken the bait. Despite the left-handed Kay opening the game, Cleveland is starting the left-handed Nathaniel Lowe at first base rather than David Fry, who started against Hagen Smith in Game 1. Similarly, the switch-hitting Patrick Bailey is behind the plate, rather than the right-handed Austin Hedges, who also started in Game 1.</p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-0a245090-c0e2-11f1-9e37-cdc3b73ee728" start="1"><li>Steven Kwan, CF</li><li>Jose Ramirez, 3B</li><li>Chase DeLauter, RF</li><li>Jo Adell, DH</li><li>Nathaniel Lowe, 1B</li><li>Angel Martinez, LF</li><li>Travis Bazzana, 2B</li><li>Patrick Bailey, C</li><li>Brayan Rocchio, SS</li></ol><p>"They've announced an opener, but we know who they have available and what it felt like today going into today's game," said Guardians manager Stephen Vogt. "This is a game Patrick Bailey is going to catch. So, it gives us the switch-hitter at the bottom to match up with the bullpen. With Nate, kind of looking at how Saturday went with only getting one at bat out of David Fry. If we're going to get one at bat out of David Fry, we'd like that in a leverage spot."</p><p>That could provide some extra incentive for Venable to stick with Kay for a bit longer than expected, two days after he threw 22 pitches in Game 1. Or, the Sox could choose to slide another left-hander in like Sean Newcomb or Noah Schultz behind Kay, before turning to Burke.</p>

entries.title: Former Illinois House GOP Leader Jim Durkin crosses party line to endorse Gov. JB Pritzker over Darren Bailey
entries.summary: <p>Former Illinois House Republican Leader Jim Durkin on Monday endorsed Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker’s reelection bid over GOP firebrand Darren Bailey, who Durkin said is “not cut out for the job.” </p><p>Encapsulating tensions within a fractured Illinois Republican Party <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/20/bob-grogan-illinois-republican-party-new-chairperson-dupage-county-auditor" target="_blank" ><u>12 years removed</u></a> from its last statewide election victory, Durkin said in a Pritzker campaign video that “it's unfortunate, but I cannot cast my vote for my party's nominee.”</p><p>“I served with Darren Bailey in Springfield, and I know what he is and isn't capable of,” said Durkin, the Western Springs Republican who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/11/10/23452445/jim-durkin-house-republican-general-assembly-trump-bailey-far-right-moderate-minority-leader-exit" target="_blank" ><u>stepped down</u></a> in 2023 after almost a decade in charge of the minority state House caucus.</p><p>“Bailey stands for exclusion over inclusion, and his politics are of subtraction over addition. His politics don't work for me, nor the Republican Party I know. He's never accomplished anything for Illinois, and he's not cut out for the job. Frankly, he cannot be trusted to lead our state.”</p><p>Durkin has long been a vocal opponent of President Donald Trump, whom the former leader blames for alienating moderate suburban voters who once provided the foundation for the Illinois GOP. Durkin chaired John McCain’s Illinois campaigns in 2000 and 2008.</p><p>Trump <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/14/trump-endorses-bailey-pritzker-illinois-governor-race" target="_blank" ><u>has endorsed Bailey</u></a>, who has distanced himself from the president as he tries to shore up Chicago area support four years after losing to Pritzker by nearly 13 percentage points.</p><p>After casting his ballot in downstate Clay County, Bailey blasted his former colleague and suggested Durkin was angling for a White House cabinet appointment from Pritzker, a potential 2028 presidential candidate.</p><p>“Jim Durkin and JB Pritzker — they don't give a damn about you, and they don't give a damn about anyone in the state of Illinois,” Bailey said, adding that he first ran for a House seat in 2018 “because Jim Durkin had failed us miserably.”</p><p>“When we ask what is wrong and how did we get here… Just disgustingly failed leaders, lead Republicans, where we’re at, like sheep to the slaughter, and here we are now,” Bailey said. “Jim Durkin never has been, never will be a Republican. He showed his true colors today.”</p><p>Durkin brushed off the barbs in an interview, rolling his eyes at “the Darren Bailey shtick.”</p><p>“He can bellyache as much as he wants about me, but I’ve done more for the party than he ever has or will,” said Durkin, who’s now an attorney advising local governments on economic issues.</p><p>“He needs to think about whether he’s value added to the GOP after November,” Durkin said. “He’s lost before. He needs to stick to what he’s best at. He’s a successful farmer.”</p><p>In the Pritzker ad, Durkin said, “I may not agree with JB on everything, but he's a good person, and he has delivered on matters important to me and to the state,” including the state’s assault weapon ban.</p><p>“I'm not going to waste my vote,” Durkin said. “I'm voting for Gov. JB Pritzker.”</p><p>In a statement, Illinois Republican Party Chair Bob Grogan said: “JB Pritzker’s two-terms as Illinois governor have been a complete and total failure as he raised our taxes over and over, championed illegal immigrants and passed the most bloated state budget in history.</p><p>“This is who opportunists in search of relevance like Jim Durkin have aligned themselves with and is further proof that the only way to save Illinois is by electing new, strong leadership like Darren Bailey,” Grogan said.</p><p>Pritzker said he “never doubted [Durkin’s] devotion to the people of our great state.”</p><p>“He was a partner in rebuilding Illinois’ infrastructure and strengthening our fiscal foundation — and an opponent of MAGA extremists driven only by their infatuation with Donald Trump,” the governor said in a statement. “Leader Durkin has the heart of a public servant, and I am honored to have his support in this campaign.”</p>

entries.title: Bears rule out QB Caleb Williams vs. Packers, will start backup Tyson Bagent again
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson won't play around with his quarterback decision this week. He said on his team-run interview Monday that starter Caleb Williams remains out with a Grade 2 hamstring strain and he will start backup Tyson Bagent again Sunday at the Packers.</p><p>Williams has been out since getting hurt late in the Sept. 20 game against the Vikings, and that type of injury usually keeps a player out at least a month. After their visit to Lambeau Field, the Bears play at the Falcons on Oct. 18 and host the Patriots on Oct. 22. Even those games could be tough for Williams, who has a better shot at returning Nov. 2 when the team visits the defending champion Seahawks.</p><p>Bagent started Sunday for the first time since 2023 and helped <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/04/bears-coach-ben-johnson-continues-to-set-himself-apart-from-predecessors-as-bears-top-jets-23-12-to-reach-3-1" >the Bears beat the Jets 23-12 to reach 3-1</a>. He completed 25 of 34 passes for 268 yards with an interception for an 83.9 passer rating, and the Bears leaned heavily on their ground game. Backup running back Kyle Monangai pounded the Jets for 146 yards an two touchdowns on 30 carries.</p>

entries.title: One public toilet? Chicago bathroom desert belies windy aspirations to being a world-class city
entries.summary: <p>It's best not to comment on specific mistaken remarks made by Mayor Brandon Johnson — the air is already thick with criticism, and once started, where does one stop? But there is one statement he says repeatedly that is almost Rahmesque in its misguided pretension:</p><p>"Chicago is a world-class city."</p><p>Yes, there is the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, the Art Institute, Margie's Candies and a few other first-rate institutions that might embolden a person to imagine Chicago is right up there with London and Paris and the other global big boys.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-090000" name="module-090000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>But the truth remains: Chicago is not a world-class city. It can't be. We don't have any public toilets. A survey by <a class="Link" href="https://nationwidewasteservice.com/the-best-and-worst-u-s-cities-for-public-toilets/" target="_blank" >Nationwide Waste Service</a> lists 21 cities. Kansas City is first, with 30 public toilets per 100,000 residents, while Chicago is dead last, with less than half, 14 per 100,000.</p><p>And those are not actual public toilets but toilets accessible to the public, theoretically, in libraries and hotels and restaurants that turn a blind eye to those in need. While a few city-run facilities no doubt lurk in remote park district field houses and other public buildings, this woeful sentence was published <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/03/chicago-self-cleaning-toilet-what-to-know?_gl=1*1l6gcyu*_up*MQ..*_gs*MQ..&gclid=Cj0KCQjw8ofWBhCHARIsANBj4Lvduq8EI5bRDhqiPUPcw1-zCiiNt4xXjaaCvpKjrjU0OvC-wO1TVTgaAhEuEALw_wcB&gbraid=0AAAAA9e-Tg6bhKezhuatFPgShX5n2Jk1Z" target="_blank" >by the Sun-Times</a> this week:</p><p>"The city’s sole public bathroom appeared near the CTA Blue Line station in the Polish Triangle at Division Street and Ashland and Milwaukee Avenues in West Town."</p><p>The structure appeared, that is. Not yet open. Almost there. After decades of dithering. Chicago is about to open one sleek self-cleaning public bathroom. In Wicker Park. How many of those are found in Paris? A city of 2 million residents, or three-quarters the population of Chicago?</p><p>Answer: 435</p><p>Any idea how embarrassing this is? How bad for our reputation? Flip open a guide book.</p><p>"Public toilets are non-existent on the streets of Chicago," a Frommer's guide chides.</p><p>How long was this humiliation in the making? (pardoning the mild pun; we journalists love punning on this topic; doing so relieves — whoops — <i>reduces</i> our discomfort.)</p><p>"Pitch for public toilets fails to flush out City Hall backing," a Tribune headline snickered in 1992, noting that JCDecaux — the same French company currently constructing the Wicker Park loo, which at the time had built 4,000 public toilet kiosks in 400 European cities and was also trying them in New York — made a presentation to obdurate Chicago administrators, who were unmoved.</p><p>"There are a lot of questions," said the city's director of central planning — cost, number, "clutter on Chicago sidewalks."</p><p>Alas, one question few bothered with — then or now — is: Where are people supposed to go to the bathroom?</p><p>"Why is this? Why in this age of issues and era of special interests is the public toilet a taboo topic?" the Trib's urban affairs columnist marveled, also in 1992. "It makes a lot of people embarrassed and unsettled."</p><p>Does it ever. Here I thought Americans were horrified at the prospect of using a bathroom where a person of indeterminate gender might be applying their lip gloss. Turns out, we're just horrified at the thought of bathrooms, period.</p><p>To be fair, Chicago does have all those alleys. And public bathrooms have a tendency to be colonized by the homeless and drug addicts — Starbucks in Europe lit their bathrooms with blue light, to prevent intravenous drug users from finding a vein. But unsavory interlopers camping out are also a problem with 24-hour ATM lobbies downtown, but one that seems mostly overcome.</p><p>We don't have public bathrooms because we don't live in a society where we recognize the duty of government to help people live decent lives. If government provided toilets, what's next? Health care?</p><p>As with health care, bathrooms represent another human necessity offloaded to private industry. Asked if Chicago needed public toilets in 1996, the president of the Oak Street Council merchants group said, "Unequivocally no. I don't think we need public toilets in Chicago. I don't think anything more is necessary to obstruct the beauty of the city. There are enough garages and hotels and restaurants around so that people can have their pick of just about any facility."</p><p>That's nonsense. Striding into Petterino's, staring down the maitre d', making a hard right and heading directly to the bathroom takes a level of moxie that most tourists with three gotta-go-now! children won't muster.</p><p>If I were looking for the bright spot, I might say: At least the pension crisis isn't the only grim Chicago reality coming home to roost after years of neglect. We spend millions urging out-of-towners to come to Chicago and explore this lovely city. And almost nothing to help them find a toilet once they get here. That doesn't scream "world class" to me.</p>

entries.title: 2 charged with Streeterville armed robbery that left man visiting from New York shot and seriously wounded
entries.summary: <p>Two individuals, including a 16-year-old boy, have been charged with shooting a man visiting from New York while they tried to rob his rental car. </p><p>Marques Williams, 22, and the teen face a slew of felony charges, including first-degree attempted murder, armed robbery with a firearm and aggravated vehicular hijacking, Chicago police said. </p><p>Williams faces an additional felony charge of possessing a weapon while being a felon, and the teen was charged with fleeing and causing more than $300 in property damage, officials said. </p><p>Williams was scheduled to appear in court Monday. Court information was not immediately available for the teen, who was charged as a juvenile. </p><p>The attack happened about 6:30 p.m. Friday in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/03/upstate-new-york-visitor-shot-streeterville-robbery" target="_blank" >400 block of East Illinois Street</a> as a man, 64, and his wife, 58, of Plattsburgh, were retrieving something from their rental car in a lower level of a garage, according to a police report obtained by the Sun-Times.</p><p>Witnesses told police two masked robbers confronted the couple, and one demanded the man give him his keys while brandishing a black gun in their direction, according to the report.</p><p>When the man refused, the gunman reportedly said, “Give me your keys, or I’m going to shoot you,” before he opened fire, hitting the man in the left side of his rib cage, according to the report.</p><p>Police and paramedics responding to the scene slowed the man’s bleeding after he was found lying on the ground. He was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital, according to the report.<br></p>

entries.title: White Sox’ Tommy Pham 'confronts' MLB commissioner Rob Manfred about baseballs
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — Tommy Pham still can’t believe the ball he hit Saturday in Game 1 of the American League Division Series didn’t leave the yard.</p><p>As an intrepid reporter was interviewing MLB commissioner Rob Manfred outside the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox’</a> dugout Monday before Game 2, Pham left his batting-practice session to ask Manfred an important question:</p><p>“Rob, what’s going on with the balls?”</p><p>“What balls?” Manfred replied.</p><p>“I can’t be hitting no-doubters, man, and not helping them in getting out,” Pham said — probably half-joking and half-serious. “How am I supposed to get a job next year if that ball don’t go out?”</p><p>The question drew laughter from Manfred and other onlookers, but it was clear what Pham still had on his mind.</p><p>In the sixth inning, Pham hit a ball 366 feet to the left-field wall with an expected batting average of .860, according to Statcast. But the wind knocked it down, Angel Martinez leaped to catch it and then he doubled off Miguel Vargas, who — like seemingly everyone else — thought the ball was gone.</p><p>“You’re on your own with the hitting-out thing,” Manfred told Pham.</p><p>Pham had been crushing the ball in batting practice, sending some into the left-field stands. He told BP pitcher Justin Jirschele about one blast, in particular.</p><p>“I said I hit that one less than the other one [Saturday], and it went out,” Pham said.</p><p>He had another question for the commissioner.</p><p>“Have you seen ‘Major League’?” Pham asked. “When Willie Mays Hayes hit the ball and he pimped it and it didn’t go out? [Someone] made a clip of me doing it. They put them together. It was funny.</p><p>“I need a good ball.”</p><p>“It’s good to see you,” Manfred said.</p><p>The conversation ended cordially, and the interview resumed — albeit awkwardly.</p><p>What does having the White Sox in the postseason mean for baseball?</p><p>“Chicago’s one of our oldest franchises, big market,” Manfred said. “They’ve struggled in recent years, and it’s a great turnaround story. It’s something that we love. It’s really good for baseball.”</p><p>Manfred was visiting the Sox for the second time this postseason as he makes his way to every major-league ballpark still hosting games.</p><p>“We started Tuesday, we went to Houston,” he said. “Then we went on to San Diego, saw them that night. Came back the next morning to Atlanta, and then got to New York in time for the Yankee game. We went to Milwaukee yesterday, and we’re here today.”</p><p>Perhaps he’ll see the Sox again — in the AL Championship Series.</p>

entries.title: Michael Jordan commits $10 million to UNC School of Social Work in honor of his mother
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> legend, six-time NBA champion and former North Carolina Tar Heels star Michael Jordan has made a $10 million commitment to the UNC School of Social Work in honor of his mother, Deloris P. Jordan.</p><p>It's the largest single gift in the School of Social Work's history and will expand the reach and impact of the Global Social Development Innovations Center, according to a release Monday. The center will be renamed the Deloris P. Jordan Global Social Development Innovations Center and the Jordan Institute for Families. It will provide financial scholarships for Master of Social Work students.</p><p>Jordan played for the Tar Heels from 1981-84, making the game-winning shot in the 1982 NCAA championship game as a freshman. He earned a bachelor of arts degree in 1986.</p><p>"My mother has always believed in the power of helping children, families and communities, and she has spent her life putting that belief into action," Jordan said in a release. "Honoring her through this gift to the UNC School of Social Work is truly meaningful to my family and to me."</p><p>Jordan said that North Carolina will always be home for him.</p><p>"I'm proud to support the social workers who are on the ground each and every day helping people navigate challenges, find opportunities and build stronger communities," Jordan said. "I hope this gift helps make it possible for more students to pursue this important work."</p><p>UNC-Chapel Hill Chancellor Lee H. Roberts said the school is grateful for Jordan's investment.</p><p>"Deloris Jordan's lifelong dedication to children and families is reflected in this investment, which will strengthen the School of Social Work's ability to improve lives across North Carolina and beyond," Roberts said.</p><p>The gift also establishes the Jordan Family Scholars program, which will provide scholarship support to Master of Social Work students facing increased financial barriers to graduate education, the release said.</p><p>Ten students will be named the inaugural Jordan Family Scholars during the celebration. Each will receive a $12,500 scholarship.</p><p>The Jordan Institute for Families (JIF) was founded in 1996 by Jordan and his family "to help cultivate safe, stable, nurturing families over the life course," according to the school. The Global Social Development Innovations center was later established in 2017 to advance innovative, evidence-informed approaches that strengthen the well-being of youth and their families.</p>

entries.title: Federal judge sides with Kalshi to block new Illinois regulations on prediction markets
entries.summary: <p>A judge has blocked Illinois from regulating prediction markets like it does sportsbooks and other gambling options, ruling that the trades offered by the likes of Kalshi and Polymarket fall under the sole jurisdiction of federal regulators even if their offerings resemble casino-style betting.</p><p>But the injunction handed down Friday in Chicago’s federal district court by Judge Martha Pacold doesn’t shut the door on potential state taxes on the profits raked in by the booming prediction market industry.</p><p>Pacold withheld a decision on that front pending further arguments over the regulatory framework that lawmakers authorized in Springfield earlier this year <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/05/31/illinois-budget-crypto-tax-prediction-markets-fantasy-sports" target="_blank" ><u>to help pass a $56 billion state budget</u></a>.</p><p>Illinois’ law calls for the state to take a percentage of transaction fees charged by prediction market companies, which offer “yes” or “no” event contracts on everything from whether the White Sox will advance to the World Series, to the weather in Chicago.</p><p>State lawmakers also ordered the companies to block traders younger than 21, while restricting offerings on sports.</p><p>The platforms function almost exactly like traditional sports betting apps, but they’re not considered gambling because users are trading against each other as opposed to playing against the “house.”</p><p>Because of that, they remain under the purview of the federal Commodity Futures Trading Commission, Pacold wrote, siding with Kalshi and its cryptocurrency partner Coinbase, which sued to block the regulations <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/06/25/kalshi-lawsuit-illinois-tax-pritzker-prediction-markets" target="_blank" ><u>in June</u></a>.</p><p>“Many of the financial instruments at issue are likely swaps as defined by the Commodity Exchange Act — they just happen to be swaps that people find entertaining and fun,” Pacold wrote. “Under the Act and precedent interpreting it, some Illinois law is likely preempted. Plaintiffs are therefore likely to succeed — at least in part.”</p><p>Pacold still signaled she’s open to upholding the state tax on transaction fees, which were originally scheduled to take effect in July. State lawmakers, anticipating the legal battle, didn’t count on revenue from the prediction market tax in their budget projections.</p><p>“The other laws Illinois seeks to enforce cause a conflict because they regulate what can be sold, as well as where it can be sold and to whom,” Pacold wrote. “Taking a cut of Kalshi and Coinbase’s profits, without more, might not pose the same conflict as regulating an entire market.”</p><p>In a social media post, Kalshi founder Luana Lopes Lara called Pacold’s ruling “beautiful.”</p><p>A spokesperson for Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul’s office declined to comment.</p><p>Illinois Gaming Board administrator Marcus Fruchter issued cease-and-desist letters in April to Kalshi and its top competitors — Polymarket, Crypto.com and Robinhood — for engaging in “illegal gambling in violation of Illinois law.”</p><p>Several other states are tussling with prediction market companies over proposed regulations, with the issue expected to eventually land before the U.S. Supreme Court.</p><p>Earlier this year, Gov. JB Pritzker signed an executive order <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/04/21/pritzker-prediction-markets-ban-illinois" target="_blank" ><u>barring state employees</u></a> from using insider information to bet on prediction markets.</p>

entries.title: Sydney Taylor to play in Unrivaled this offseason
entries.summary: <p>It’s official: Sydney Taylor is playing in Unrivaled.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> guard was one of four players announced today as Unrivaled finalized their 50-player roster. Taylor is signed to a multi-year contract, according to the league.</p><p>Taylor has already wowed in the 3-on-3 format as a member of USA Basketball's U23 team. Unrivaled's format is different than international 3-on-3, but the bigger court should actually suit Taylor's speed. It will also force her to improve her defense, a necessary growth point for the AP All-Rookie team selection. </p><p>At Unrivaled she’ll be joining several Sky players including Skylar Diggins, Kate Martin, Natasha Cloud, and Gabriela Jaquez (development pool). Sky forward Rickea Jackson is also signed to a multi-year deal with the league but will miss the 2027 season while recovering from an ACL injury.</p><p>Season 3 of Unrivaled kicks off Jan. 8. The biggest shift this season is that the league will be playing more games on the road rather than at their primary arena in Miami. Tour stops have been announced in Boston, Inglewood, Detroit, San Francisco, Brooklyn, Minneapolis, Houston, and Philadelphia.</p><p>Unrivaled was founded in 2024 by WNBA stars Breanna Stewart and Napheesa Collier as an opportunity for elite players to stay stateside. Taylor initially planned to play with the Turkish club Galatasaray this offseason, but ultimately opted for Unrivaled when the opportunity presented itself. </p>

entries.title: Comienza la votación temprana y por correo en Chicago para las elecciones intermedias de noviembre
entries.summary: <p>En cuanto Justin Labonte tuvo la edad suficiente para votar, se propuso emitir su voto. Desde entonces, no se ha perdido ninguna elección.</p><p>Labonte, de 30 años de edad, estuvo entre los primeros en llegar el jueves por la mañana al supersitio Chicago Voting Supersite, en el 137 S.
