entries.title: Lime warns Divvy deal could push company from Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Scooter-share company Lime wants Chicago to pump the brakes on its Divvy expansion proposal, warning the deal could monopolize the city's micromobility system under current operator Lyft and lead to higher prices.</p><p>Lime says the ordinance gives Divvy and Lyft "an unfair, government-sanctioned advantage," and called to delay a potential committee vote on Friday, according to a drafted letter to Pedestrian and Traffic Safety Committee Chair Ald. Daniel La Spata (1st).</p><p>Lime, in a separate statement, said the proposed deal could kill competition with the only remaining scooter-share company and force it from the city.</p><p>Lime is the only other rental scooter operator in Chicago, besides Lyft. The city initially gave e-scooter licenses to two other companies, Spin and Superpedestrian, in 2021. Superpedestrian <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/9/7/23863321/superpedestrian-scooter-chicago-market" target="_blank" >pulled its scooters</a> from the city in 2023, citing stiff competition with Lyft. Spin <a class="Link" href="https://wgntv.com/news/traffic/what-to-know-before-riding-a-shared-scooter-in-chicago/" target="_blank" >reportedly</a> stopped operating its scooters last year.</p><p>"This proposal as currently written would actually create a monopoly for Lyft by making it impossible for Lime to operate a successful program," Lime spokesman Jacob Tugendrajch told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Last month, Johnson's office announced <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/23/chicago-extends-divvy-contract-with-changes-to-parking-and-new-bike-model-coming" target="_blank" >its plan</a> to extend Lyft's contract by five years beyond 2028, when the current agreement ends. The plan gives half-off Divvy discounts to rides on the South and West sides, and expands Divvy's "core area" where it places docks, bikes and scooters — though the city has not shared specific boundaries.</p><p>The city has contracted Lyft to operate Divvy, the city's bike- and scooter-share system, since 2019. The Divvy system, which includes docking stations, bikes and scooters, has been owned by the city's Department of Transportation since Divvy's launch in 2013. Lime operates only scooters in Chicago, according to its own agreement with the city.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson is sponsoring the Divvy ordinance. In a statement, Johnson's office said it appreciates Lime's investment in the city.</p><p>"With a focus on building upon our progress fostering an equitable micro mobility ecosystem, the administration will continue to engage with industry partners and members of the City Council as the legislative process plays out," the mayor's office said.</p><p>La Spata and Lyft did not immediately respond to requests for comment.</p><p>Lime said it wants the city to rewrite the Divvy deal to "address monopoly concerns."</p><p>The company also asked the city to consider its proposed automatic pricing discount for low-income residents. Lime said Lyft's current low-income discount pricing is 34% higher than that of Lime's own access program, and that Divvy's prices are 19% higher than Lime's on the South and West sides.</p><p>In New York City, where Lyft operates the city's bike-share program Citi Bike, Lime said the company has a "geographical monopoly" that has led to <a class="Link" href="https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/08/12/deep-dive-cheaper-citi-bike-will-need-more-than-public-subsidy" target="_blank" >higher prices</a>. The state's comptroller has also <a class="Link" href="https://www.osc.ny.gov/files/state-agencies/audits/pdf/sga-2026-23n5.pdf" target="_blank" >called out the company</a> for not paying the city everything it was owed.</p><p>In Chicago, Lime asked the city to share the expected costs of the proposed Divvy extension, and to share revenue numbers of all bike- and scooter-share companies.</p><p>Despite the city prohibiting Lime scooters in the Central Business District, where only Divvy can operate, Lime said its scooters logged 6.1 million rides last year. That's slightly less than <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/mayor/press_room/press_releases/2026/january/micromobility-record-year.html" target="_blank" >6.8 million rides</a> last year on Divvy scooters and bikes.</p>

entries.title: Ticket prices are soaring for White Sox home playoff game
entries.summary: <p>If White Sox fans want to walk through the gates at Rate Field on Wednesday, they'll need to get their hands on the priciest ticket in the divisional series round, according to several national ticket broker sites.</p><p>A single ticket on TickPick for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >Sox</a> and Guardians American League Division Series matchup jumped to $327 on Monday, up from $250 Thursday, making it the most expensive American or National League Division Series game on its platform — a surprising ascension considering the star power and markets of some of the remaining teams, including the Dodgers, Yankees and Padres.</p><p>“Chicago fans are showing early on that they’re hungry for playoff baseball and depending on the outcome of this series, we’d expect that demand to carry through their postseason run,” Kyle Zorn, director of content at New York City-based TickPick, said. “When you consider that White Sox fans watched this team post the worst record in modern MLB history just two seasons ago and now they’re watching them compete in the ALDS, that turnaround is going to help set the floor for ticket prices in Chicago as the postseason continues.”</p><p>The club’s historic turnaround — fueled by young, rising stars and other team castaways — has been nothing short of remarkable, with the Sox entering the 2026 season with three straight years of at least 100 losses, including a modern day record 121 losses in 2024.</p><p>Meanwhile, the average purchase price for Game 3 on TickPick continues to rise and could end up as the most expensive Sox ticket in five years. The team last hosted a Game 3 in the ALDS in 2021 against the Astros, when the average ticket price was $242.</p><p>StubHub has sold nearly twice as many tickets for Wednesday's game compared to an average regular-season home game, with the get-in price at $310 on Monday. Prices were slightly higher on Saturday at $336.</p><p>Game 3 has a price premium of roughly 330% over the team’s regular season average price, with fans paying four times the price for a typical Sox ticket.</p><p>The premium is also the most of any home team in a divisional series playoff, with the Brewers and Padres a distant second with premiums of 230% to 280%, according to the New York City-based ticketing platform.</p><p>"White Sox fans are celebrating their first playoff series win since 2005, and the demand shows it,” Jill Gonzalez, StubHub’s head of consumer, product and tech communications, said.</p><p>The game is also the most expensive of the 12 guaranteed divisional series games on TicketNetwork, according to the Connecticut-based platform.</p><p>The cheapest get-in price soared to $464 by Monday afternoon, that's slightly up from $421 on Saturday afternoon after the Sox beat the Guardians 3-0 in Game 1. Friday morning ticket prices hovered at $269.</p><p>And the average ticket price is about $792, well above the median price of $620, TicketNetwork shows.</p><p>In terms of tickets sold, the average ticket price was about $366, or 78% higher than the 2021 game against the Astros, which hit $206.</p><p>Demand for this year’s Sox home playoff tickets on TicketNetwork are much higher than that of other teams. Overall prices for the other ALDS and NLDS games are comparable to recent years, from 2021 to 2025, but the anomaly are Sox games, which are outpacing all others by a wide margin.</p><p>The next closest get-in price for a divisional series home game was $179 for Game 1 at Cleveland’s Progressive Field, which was likely bolstered by the well-traveled Sox fan base, which were heard cheering throughout the game’s broadcast.</p><p>“What’s unusual this year isn’t the division series market as a whole — it’s Chicago,” Sean Burns, TicketNetwork’s director of communications and public affairs, said. “When a fan base has waited a long time for a meaningful home playoff moment, that can create its own kind of premium.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/05/white-sox-set-lineup-for-game-2-alds-matchup-against-guardians-and-right-hander-gavin-williams-tristan-peters-will-venable-sean-burke-anthony-kay-colson-montgomery-braden-montgomery" >White Sox set lineup for ALDS Game 2 matchup against Guardians and right-hander Gavin Williams</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Finance Committee backs $260.8M settlement resolving cases tied to former cop Reynaldo Guevara
entries.summary: <p>For the second time in 12 months, the City Council’s Finance Committee has authorized what one alderman called a “gigantic but responsible” settlement to compensate victims of a sordid chapter in the history of the Chicago Police Department.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/10/01/brandon-johnson-proposed-global-settlement-police-misconduct-cases-ex-cpd-det-reynaldo-guevara" >$260.8 million global settlement</a> approved Monday by a unanimous voice vote would resolve16 police misconduct lawsuits and compensate 17 plaintiffs framed for murders by corrupt former Chicago police Detective Reynaldo Guevara. That amounts to nearly $680,000 for every one of the nearly 384 years that the recipients spent in prison.</p><p>All 17 murder convictions — involving events dating as far back as 1987 — were subsequently vacated. All but two of the defendants got certificates of innocence. At the time they were arrested for murder, the plaintiffs were between the ages of 14 and 28. Each spent an average of 22.6 years in prison.</p><p>The settlement would be paid out over two years in four, $65 million installments. It still needs approval from the full Council. </p><p>It nearly triples the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/10/02/victims-90-million-dollars-police-misconduct-settlement-chicago-police-ronald-watts" target="_blank" >$90 million global settlement</a> that put to rest 176 lawsuits tied to former Chicago Police Sgt. Ronald Watts, who was accused of framing hundreds of people on drug charges at the Chicago Housing Authority’s Ida B. Wells complex.</p><p>The bad news for beleaguered Chicago taxpayers is there’s more where that came from.</p><p>Monday’s payout and “two more in the queue," as Deputy Corporation Counsel Jessica Felker put it, will only resolve half of the pending Guevara cases. The other 23 cases will almost certainly require a similarly large settlement.</p><p>Already, the Guevara scandal is by far the costliest in police department history. It more than doubles the $210 million in settlements, judgments, legal fees and reparations stemming from the torture era of former Area 2 Cmdr. Jon Burge and his midnight crew.</p><p>“Although this mass settlement is a tremendous amount of money, the city’s potential liability is at least double if these cases were sent to trial,” Felker told the Finance Committee.</p><p>“In that circumstance, the estimated exposure is well over half a billion dollars. That includes $20 million to $25 million in fees for outside counsel, and if plaintiffs were to prevail at trial, $60 million to $70 million in plaintiffs’ counsel fees.”</p><p>Finance Committee members agreed with that assessment even as they acknowledged it will be a bitter pill for taxpayers to swallow.</p><p>“Nobody hates signing off on $260 million based on the fiscal mess that we have more than me,” said 34th Ward Ald. Bill Conway, a former Cook County prosecutor.</p><p>"But … we have a significant unknown liability here, and this takes a lot of it off the books. … I would ask my colleagues to support this gigantic but responsible settlement.”</p><p>Ald. Ray Lopez (15th) said he, too, would “bite my tongue and do it” even though “this body is saying yes without knowing whether we actually have the money to pay for it.”</p><p>“I find this good and bad — revolting, yet necessary,” said Lopez, one of the Council’s staunchest police supporters. “As someone who has voted against these [Guevara] settlements as recently as our last meeting — when we know that there’s questions of people's certificates of innocence or even those without them, swallowing this is like bad medicine because I know there are still outstanding questions.”</p><p>Lopez asked Felker how the city planned to pay for what he called the “largest settlement in U.S. history."</p><p>Felker would only say that the $260.8 million was part of the Law Department’s budget forecast for 2027 and 2028 and that the money would not be borrowed.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson’s projected $882 million budget shortfall includes an unprecedented $401 million for legal settlements.</p><p>South Side 20th Ward Ald. Jeanette Taylor said she was angered to learn that Guevara, who retired from the police department in June 2005, was still collecting a pension for the 30 years he spent on the police force.</p><p>“State law currently says the only reason you can take away somebody’s pension is if they are convicted of a felony in the scope of their employment,” Felker told Taylor.</p><p>When Taylor asked what has changed to “make sure stuff like this doesn’t happen again,” Felker told her, "A lot." </p><p>Perhaps the most significant change is the fact that police interrogations are videotaped “from beginning to end” to prevent coercion and physical, verbal or psychological abuse. </p><p>Ald. Rosanna Rodriguez-Sanchez (33rd) said the financial burden heaped upon taxpayers is "incredibly unfortunate."</p><p>But she added, "I also need us to be very aware of the human cost. ... It's 383 years of prison for people who didn't commit a crime." </p><p>To date, at least 57 people with convictions tied to Guevara have been exonerated, according to court records and the National Registry of Exonerations. All but four were murder convictions.</p><p>The city of Chicago, Cook County and the state of Illinois have already paid the exonerees nearly $185 million in settlements, jury awards and compensation, a WBEZ analysis found. The nearly $261 million in settlements on the Council's Finance Committee agenda Monday would increase the sum to nearly $446 million.</p><p><i>Contributing: WBEZ reporter Chip Mitchell</i></p>

entries.title: Bulls Josh Giddey knows a thing or two about that ugly word 'rebuild'
entries.summary: <p>It’s a word that’s been thrown around freely since executive vice president of basketball operations Bryson Graham was hired by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> ownership: “Rebuild.”</p><p>A bad word in some locker rooms, a word that offers up hope in others.</p><p>It comes down to perspective and point guard Josh Giddey has a wide one.</p><p>“I’ve been a part of (a rebuild), so I feel like I know how the whole thing goes,” Giddey said of his days in Oklahoma City. “I’ve been on a team that was the No. 1 seed, I’ve been on a team that was the lowest seed in the league, so it’s not something that is completely foreign to me. But I think with this group, I think it’s a young team but a talented team. We’ve got a good mix of veterans and younger guys, so in terms of my role, as the point guard you want to be a leader, you want to be an extension of the coach on the court, and make sure the guys are on the same page. I think it’s my job to put guys in position to be successful, so that might look different on any given night.”</p><p>And that will be one of the keys for this Bulls season to turn from “rebuild” to promise — consistency.</p><p>Giddey is the focal point of that considering he has the ball in his hands, and while he’s had stretches on both ends of the floor with consistency there is still clean-up to be done.</p><p>Tiago Splitter pulled no punches with that when asked about Giddey, as the coach made it very clear that his turnover numbers needed to dwindle.</p><p>The offense will still be up-tempo like it was under Billy Donovan, and Giddey was coming off a season in which the turnovers jumped up from 2.9 per game in the 2024-25 campaign to 3.6 per game last year.</p><p>What will help with those numbers going down? Giddey being less careless but also having more competent players around him.</p><p>Veteran Norman Powell helps with that, as does aggressive rim-runners like Matas Buzelis and Nic Claxton. Claxton did tweak his hamstring so will be on the shelf for a few weeks, according to Splitter, but is one of the more explosive centers Giddey has had in a few years.</p><p>Then there’s rookie Caleb Wilson, who gives Giddey one of the better athletes he’s played with. Yes, the No. 4 overall pick is only 20 and is yet to play a regular-season NBA game but has impressed Giddey since he first watched Wilson play Summer League games in Las Vegas.</p><p>“It’s obviously a different kind of level when you play against real NBA talent in the regular season, but one thing he doesn’t lack is confidence and that’s a real good skillset to have as a high draft pick,” Giddey said of the rookie. “Obviously, there is a lot of external pressure on him from the media, and it just comes naturally with being such a high draft pick, but unbelievable work ethic. He’s someone that anytime I’m there late at night, he’s always in the gym. He’s always in early, leaves late, so for a guy like that with as much talent as him, to work as hard as he does, that’s probably his special talent and something that will make him better as a player.”</p><p>And that’s why Giddey isn’t dwelling on the word “rebuild” as an anchor around his ankle. He knows that this Bulls roster has its holes, but he also sees a group of players that might be overlooked.</p><p>“Like I said, consistency is going to be important,” he added. “To put a ceiling on this team would be the wrong thing to do because internally we believe that what’s in this locker room is good enough to compete every night.”</p>

entries.title: Chicago woman shot by Border Patrol files lawsuit challenging feds’ narrative
entries.summary: <p>The federal immigration agent who repeatedly shot <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" >Marimar Martinez</a> one year ago fired his final shot into the rear passenger window of her fleeing vehicle as she crouched against her steering wheel, her attorneys revealed Monday while announcing a lawsuit.</p><p>The detail comes from a forensic reconstruction her attorneys are using to support Martinez’s highly anticipated lawsuit against the federal government. She is suing over her Oct. 4, 2025, shooting<b> </b>by<b> </b>Border Patrol agent Charles<b> </b>Exum in Brighton Park — and the failed prosecution that followed.</p><p>She joined her attorneys for a downtown news conference to discuss the reconstruction<b> </b>and litigation.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" >Marimar Martinez, shot by Border Patrol in Chicago, speaks out after Good, Pretti deaths: ‘I am their voice’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>It’s another step in the broader push for accountability one year after Operation Midway Blitz. The Trump administration deportation campaign that hit Chicago last fall has prompted several lawsuits and a bid for criminal charges against agents like the one who shot Martinez.</p><p>So far, no Midway Blitz agent has faced criminal charges for on-duty conduct.</p><p>The Chicago Police Department has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/08/25/marimar-martinez-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-chicago-police-cpd" target="_blank" >begun to investigate</a> Martinez’s shooting, though. And the probe has been assigned to a unit staffed with experienced detectives who will look to bring a case to Cook County prosecutors, the Chicago Sun-Times has reported.</p><p>Now, Martinez and her lawyers are moving forward with their own efforts. Their reconstruction of the shooting scene further undermines the feds’ original claim that Martinez and another man “rammed”<b> </b>agents with their vehicles and that Martinez<b> </b>drove her vehicle toward Exum.</p><p>Martinez’s lawyers said the analysis shows Exum fired three shots into<b> </b>the<b> </b>windshield of Martinez’s Nissan Rogue, another into the front passenger side and a fifth through the rear passenger side.</p><p>At Monday's news conference, lawyer Michael Gallagher said his team's experts have “objective proof that this was a bad shoot. That everything Exum said was a lie. And most importantly, Marimar is telling the truth.”</p><p>Christopher Parente, another lawyer for Martinez, insisted that his client's shooting isn't a political issue.</p><p>“We are asking the Department of Justice to do something," he told reporters. "It’s not the Department of Republicans. It’s not the Department of Democrats.”</p><p>Martinez, a U.S. citizen born<b> </b>and raised in Chicago, suffered seven wounds<b> </b>but survived. She began to prominently criticize the Trump administration’s deportation campaign early this year,<b> </b>after immigration authorities in Minneapolis fatally shot Renee Good and Alex Chicago U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros’ office also brought charges against her of assaulting a federal agent — only to drop those charges 46 days later.</p><p>Still, Martinez’s lawyers say a trove of evidence from that prosecution shows Exum<b> </b>lied to justify shooting Martinez.</p><p>"Who’s the real domestic terrorist?” Parente asked at the news conference, after presenting some of the evidence. </p><p>The Illinois Accountability Commission concluded in April that Exum “shot an unarmed civilian without apparent justification”; that<b> </b>“evidence was deliberately tampered with and destroyed”; and<b> </b>“federal agents produced materially inaccurate official reports.”</p><p>Martinez did have a firearm with her that day, but it was inside a snapped-closed<b> </b>bright pink holster at the bottom of her purse, court records show.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker, who established the commission, wrote on social media this weekend that Martinez<b> </b>“deserves true justice and accountability from the federal government.”</p><p>Martinez’s shooting was also cited in a lawsuit filed early this year by the state of Illinois and city of Chicago against Homeland Security. It alleges Midway Blitz was designed to coerce the state and city into assisting the federal government with its deportation efforts.</p><p>A federal judge has said she will decide Nov. 17<b> </b>whether to let that lawsuit move forward.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/08/25/marimar-martinez-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-chicago-police-cpd" >Elite Chicago police unit now investigating Border Patrol shooting of Marimar Martinez, source says</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Martinez crossed paths with Exum roughly one month into the Midway Blitz campaign. She said she’d been on her way to donate clothing at a church when she spotted a Chevrolet Tahoe driven by Exum that carried two additional agents.</p><p>She followed the SUV, honked her horn, yelled<b> </b>“la migra”<b> </b>and tried to warn people nearby.</p><p>She said she pulled her Rogue beside the Tahoe near 39th Street and Kedzie Avenue, where she said Exum swerved<b> </b>and their vehicles swiped each other.</p><p>Body-camera footage appears to show Exum<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/10/marimar-martinez-the-chicago-woman-shot-by-border-patrol-agent-expected-to-file-lawsuit-release-evidence" target="_blank" >turning his steering wheel<b> </b>to the left</a>, toward Martinez’s car before the collision.</p><p>Martinez said she stopped her Rogue but feared being “manhandled”<b> </b>by the agents, so she drove away. She said she veered to her “farthest left”<b> </b>to avoid the agents<b> </b>climbing out of their vehicle on her right. As she passed, she said she saw their guns.</p><p>She said she “shrugged,”<b> </b>scrunching her body against the steering wheel. And she heard shots fired.</p><p>Martinez pulled over at a repair shop, was taken to a hospital and eventually into federal custody.</p><p>Meanwhile, Exum wrote<b> </b>in text messages after the shooting that his superiors<b> </b>had been supportive of him. Then-U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino<b> </b>even offered to put off Exum’s retirement following his “excellent service in Chicago,”<b> </b>one email shows.</p><p>Another supporter told Exum<b> </b>in a text message, “you are a legend among agents you better f---in know that.”</p><p>“Beers on me when I see you at training.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/3e/79/71b60db147428d8edf68a2e6e2c5/martinezvusa.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Review: Doja Cat struts, slinks and shakes through her energetic, femme-forward show
entries.summary: <p>Grammy Award-winning rapper/singer/pop star Doja Cat has broken the mold on what it means to be a rap superstar since her 2018 debut album “Amala.” Latto, the first platinum-selling female rap artist from Atlanta and an alum of the reality show “The Rap Game,” joins Doja’s “Tour Ma Vie” world tour, pairing two biracial rappers (both with white mothers and Black fathers).</p><p>Both artists have honed their craft since childhood; both are known for their curves and rump shaking in their videos and concerts; and both have pushed boundaries in hip hop with their music while navigating their privilege as fairer-skinned women. Combining their superpowers at the United Center on Saturday, they sent a message to the world that women are the dominant forces in hip hop today.</p><p>First up was Latto, who released her fourth album “Big Mama” in May and collaborated with Doja Cat on her Billboard chart-topping single “Okayyy.” In a cheetah-print leotard with her curves on full display, she went straight into attack mode with her own band and dancers dressed in all black. With her commanding voice, she ripped through the song “Big Mama,” where she performed with her near-life-size mascot, a caricature of herself, dancing beside her.</p><p>One of the most touching moments was her verse from “POP IT,” a 2025 collaboration with her romantic partner and Grammy Award-winning rapper 21 Savage; it opened with a video of her and 21 bonding with their newborn child. When she performed her mighty anthem “B**** from the Souf” with only her voice and a thunderous band, the whole arena roared with every word.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Doja Cat, donning an ’80s-inspired spandex outfit with red accessories, came out swinging with “Cards.”</p><p>Doja’s creative approach to her songs and the show’s musical direction felt like a celebratory homage to her influences. From the neon-colored suits to the otherworldly live band of mostly Black musicians, the show was a rare mix of Madonna-esque 1980s pop meets early ’90s <a class="Link" href="https://barrymichaelc.medium.com/teddy-rileys-new-jack-swing-harlem-gangsters-raise-a-genius-1f441da4e7f1" target="_blank" ><u>New Jack Swing</u></a>, a fusion genre pioneered by <a class="Link" href="https://www.revolt.tv/article/2017-10-23/45416/groove-me-the-story-of-new-jack-swing" target="_blank" ><u>Teddy Riley</u></a> that blended traditional R&B and funk with hip-hop beats. Songs like the empowering “Woman” and “Say So” were refreshed as New Jack Swing, elevating the music to new heights.</p><p>Latto returned to the stage with Doja Cat to perform “Okayyy,” their song from Latto’s album “Big Mama.” Their chemistry was on full display as they traded bars and twerk moves on the long runway.</p><p>Body positivity was an underlying theme between Latto and Doja Cat, who donned figure-revealing spandex and shook it all profusely. Thanks to the big screens at the United Center, the lucky fans caught every angle.</p><p>They’re spitting on decades of sexism and body shaming toward Black women in music who historically have been held to white-centric beauty standards magnified by social media. In a 2023 interview on the <a class="Link" href="http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u-DLQVmg6cM" target="_blank" ><u>Angie Martinez</u></a> show, Latto got real about how attacks against women for their natural body changes take a tremendous toll on women’s mental health.</p><p>“So, when they be like, ‘Oh, she gained weight,’ I’d be like, damn, I need to get on a treadmill. That stuff does mess with your head,” Latto explained to Martinez. “It’s just women in general. We’re held to a standard like you gotta look like you just stepped off a magazine at all times. Coincidentally (or, was it?), she held a whipped-cream pie, saying he had the “perfect face” for it.</p><p>“It’s almost like you planned for this. entries.title: Bears-Packers: Sunday is Ben Johnson's chance to back up what he screamed in January
entries.summary: <p>The last time <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson faced the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/05/bears-rule-out-qb-caleb-williams-vs-packers-will-start-backup-tyson-bagent-again" target="_blank" >Packers</a>, he gathered his players in the locker room following a come-from-behind playoff win and laid his feelings bare.</p><p></p><p>“F--- the Packers,” he said. “F--- them. F---ing hate those guys.”</p><p></p><p>He didn’t apologize for it, either.</p><p></p><p>"This is a rivalry," he said later. "And [for] the city of Chicago, Green Bay, it needs to be a rivalry."</p><p></p><p>There were no F-bombs thrown around in Sunday’s postgame speech — “You guys know what next week is? Enough said,” Johnson said — and no bulletin board material to come from the coach Monday, either. In fact, Johnson seemed relieved to have finished his Zoom call with reporters without igniting a firestorm in advance of Sunday’s game at Lambeau Field.</p><p></p><p>Receiver Luther Burden knows Johnson’s true feelings.</p><p></p><p>“I feel like he wants to beat them really bad,” Burden said. “Like everybody else in the room, every Chicago fan. We just want to beat them real bad and make them quit.”</p><p></p><p>Johnson circled the Packers game on his first day on the job. In his introductory press conference, he quipped that he enjoyed beating Matt LaFleur twice a year as a Lions assistant coach. LaFleur was bewildered that Johnson, whom he doesn’t know well, would make the comment. The two have exchanged quips through the media since, and their icy relationship is never more apparent than during a postgame handshake in which neither man breaks stride.</p><p></p><p>LaFleur was asked Monday why he rarely inserted himself into the rivalry discourse. His answer could be interpreted as a passing shot at the opposing coach, who has.</p><p></p><p>“This game is about players,” he told Green Bay reporters. “We'll keep it about the players. I'm not the one out there playing. That's always been my mentality.”</p><p></p><p>Johnson and LaFleur are the faces of the rivalry, though, particularly with stars Caleb Williams and Micah Parsons out with injuries. And their franchises appear to be heading in opposite directions.</p><p></p><p>On Dec. 7, the Packers beat the Bears at Lambeau Field when Williams threw an interception in the end zone with 22 seconds to play. The Packers then lost their last five games — including two at Soldier Field, one in the regular season and then in the playoffs. Their two wins this season have come in overtime against a Jets team the Bears beat by 11 and, on Sunday, a Buccaneers team starting an undrafted rookie quarterback for the first time. LaFleur, who received a contract extension shortly after losing in last year’s playoffs, has drawn the ire of a typically supportive fan base.</p><p></p><p>The Bears, by contrast, lost in the second round of the playoffs last year and have opened the season 3-1 despite playing three different quarterbacks.</p><p></p><p>With Johnson calling plays, the Bears have outscored their opponents by 47 points, the third-best margin in the league through Sunday’s games. The Packers have been outscored by 32, the fourth-most.</p><p></p><p>The Bears have scored the ninth-most points. The Packers have scored the sixth-fewest. The Bears lead the league in yards gained. The Packers are 19th.</p><p></p><p>Before the Bears beat their rivals 31-27 in the wild card round of last year’s playoffs, the Packers had lost just three of the previous 20 rivalry matchups and seven of 37. The Bears have thought they’ve turned the tide before, though, only for the Packers to, the next year, prove them wrong.</p><p></p><p>Matt Nagy beat the Packers at Soldier Field to clinch the NFC North in 2018. He opened the season against them the following year and lost 10-3, starting a stretch of 11-straight Bears losses to the Packers. John Fox stunned the Packers at Lambeau Field in 2015 then lost his next four rivalry games by a combined 47 points before being fired. Marc Trestman won at Soldier Field in his first rivalry game and lost the next three by 67 points before being canned.</p><p></p><p>Johnson split the two regular season games against the Packers last year before beating them in the playoffs. Amazingly, he owns more wins against the rival than any Bears coach since Lovie Smith. Nagy, Fox and Trestman each won once, as did interim Thomas Brown. Matt Eberflus went 0-5.</p><p></p><p>A win at Lambeau Field would provide another clue that things are changing. Lose, and it feels like more of the same.</p><p></p><p>Bears chairman George McCaskey knows the stakes. At the NFL’s annual meeting in April, he said he was fine with Johnson’s feelings about the Packers, cursing and all, but knew that “you gotta back it up” on the field.</p><p></p><p>“If we don’t beat them in the playoffs, then the narrative is still, ‘Well, you still can’t get past them. …’” McCaskey told the Sun-Times then. “The rivalry is 100 plus years old. And, sad to say, the last 30 years they’ve had the better of us.”</p><p></p><p>Sunday is Johnson’s first chance to back up the words he screamed in January.</p><p></p><p>“This is a big week for us,” Johnson said. “It’s important to our organization, it’s important to theirs as well. It’ll be really good competition here on Sunday.”<br></p>

entries.title: With new dad Bowen Byram back in fold, Blackhawks hope to stabilize defense
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> defenseman Bowen Byram got the call from his pregnant wife, Kailey, around 5:30 a.m. Saturday morning: He needed to get back to Chicago.</p><p>Byram quickly left the Hawks' team hotel in Buffalo, landed in Chicago around 10:30 a.m. and was at the hospital when Kailey gave birth to twin girls — their first children — around 3:20 p.m.</p><p>"It was definitely a crazy day, but I was happy I was able to get back and support her through it," Byram said Monday.</p><p>"Everything went smoothly. They came a little earlier than we would've liked, but they're doing great. Everything has been going super well."</p><p>The 25-year-old Canadian returned to practice Monday, having unfortunately missed the Hawks' <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/03/blackhawks-sabres-loss-bowen-byram-louis-crevier" >defeat</a> Saturday against his former Sabres teammates, and should be in the lineup Tuesday for the Hawks' home opener against the Blues.</p><p>"Even just getting off the ice today for practice, I'm so excited to go back and see my baby girls," he added. "I feel like whenever you go through a major life change, it puts things in perspective. I'm super excited."</p><p>The so-called "new dad boost" is a famous phenomenon around the NHL, and Byram is hoping to experience one of his own this week.</p><p>He and the Hawks could use it, considering their opening road trip could hardly have gone worse. They're 0-3-0 to start a season for the first time since 2021, having been cumulatively outscored 15-5 and outshot 97-56.</p><p>Byram liked that the Hawks "got going" by the third period against the Golden Knights, but he admitted the blowout loss to the Mammoth was a "not one of my prouder moments."</p><p>"We had a tough night," he said. "Obviously, you're going to have those throughout the season. Do you expect them to be game two? No. But it happened. You've got to own it like a man and try to get better. That's what we've done and will continue to do."</p><p>During the preseason, Byram impressively <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/22/blackhawks-bowen-byram-swagger-confidence-preseason" >demonstrated</a> his ability to anticipate puck movement with elite vision and get there first with elite skating.</p><p>Those skills weren't as evident in Las Vegas and Salt Lake City, which led to him getting out-muscled and out-played. The Hawks were outscored 3-0 and outshot 25-11 during his five-on-five ice time. It would be understandable if his focus was partly elsewhere then, though.</p><p>Hawks coach Jeff Blashill switched up the defensive pairings halfway through the Salt Lake debacle, and it's those combinations that will start together Tuesday: Byram with Artyom Levshunov, Alex Vlasic with Ian Cole and Wyatt Kaiser with Sam Rinzel.</p><p>Byram has moved back to his natural left side while fellow lefty Cole has shifted over to the right, where he does have plenty of experience. The Hawks will need either Byram or Cole to play on their off side every game, since Levshunov and Rinzel are their only natural righties.</p><p>Blashill hopes splitting apart Byram and Vlasic — arguably the Hawks' two best defensemen — brings more stability to the unit.</p><p>"You'll have one of those two guys out there for anywhere from 40 to 50 minutes...if they're not playing on the same 'D' pair," Blashill said. "There's an advantage in that."</p><p>With their next two games against teams that missed the playoffs last season and eight of their next nine games at home, the Hawks need to right their ship right now.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Connor Bedard taking part in skating/shooting drills with the Blackhawks in practice: <a href="https://t.co/4qVtxUsPTL">pic.twitter.com/4qVtxUsPTL</a></p>— Ben Pope (@BenPopeCST) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCST/status/2107140953509105869?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 5, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Although Connor Bedard can't help them right now, he is inching closer to readiness, which could boost morale for everyone else.</p><p>Wearing a non-contact jersey, Bedard participated in a couple team drills during practice Monday for the first time since undergoing shoulder surgery in July. The Hawks haven't shared any timeline updates, but it seems conceivable he could return by the end of October.</p><p>"It's awesome to have [Bedard] out there," Blashill said.</p>
